plant.description: • Hummingbird Mint (Agastache spp.) is a fragrant ornamental herb in the mint family. It is generally considered safe for cats and is not listed as a toxic plant by major veterinary poison references such as the ASPCA. As with any plant that is not part of a cat's normal diet, eating a large amount may cause mild, self-limiting stomach upset, but serious poisoning is not expected from the whole plant.

basics.description: • Hummingbird Mint (Agastache spp.) is a fragrant ornamental herb in the mint family. It is generally considered safe for cats and is not listed as a toxic plant by major veterinary poison references such as the ASPCA. As with any plant that is not part of a cat's normal diet, eating a large amount may cause mild, self-limiting stomach upset, but serious poisoning is not expected from the whole plant.

symptoms.name: Vomiting and Diarrhea
symptoms.notes: Eating any plant that is not part of a cat's normal diet can cause mild, self-limiting stomach upset. This is not a documented toxicosis specific to Hummingbird Mint and is expected to be transient.

symptoms.name: Drooling or Foaming at the Mouth
symptoms.notes: Hypersalivation can occur as a transient reaction to the strong taste of the plant. It is not a documented toxic effect of Hummingbird Mint.

treatments.name: Induction of Emesis (Vomiting) or Gastric Lavage
treatments.description: ◦ Emesis: If the ingestion was recent (typically within 1–2 hours), a veterinarian may administer prescription medication (such as xylazine or dexmedetomidine) to induce vomiting and remove the plant material from the stomach24. ◦ Gastric Lavage: In more extreme cases where a large amount was consumed, the vet may perform a "stomach pump" procedure to wash out the stomach contents23. ◦ Activated Charcoal: Following emesis or lavage, activated charcoal may be administered to bind any remaining toxins in the gastrointestinal tract and prevent further absorption.
treatments.notes: Critical Warning: You should never attempt to induce vomiting at home using hydrogen peroxide. While some older sources might suggest it, current veterinary guidelines state it can cause severe injury to a cat's mouth, throat, and stomach4. Decontamination should only be performed by a veterinary professional.

treatments.name: Intravenous (IV) Fluids
treatments.description: The veterinarian administers fluids directly into the bloodstream to correct dehydration caused by persistent vomiting or diarrhea. This also helps to flush toxins from the body and support liver and kidney function.
treatments.notes: This is particularly important if the cat has become dehydrated or is showing signs of shock or weakness.

treatments.name: Anti-emetics and Gastroprotectants
treatments.description: ◦ Anti-emetics: Medications are given to stop severe or prolonged vomiting2. ◦ Gastroprotectants/Antacids: Medication is administered to coat the stomach lining and reduce acid, soothing the gastrointestinal irritation caused by the mint oils.
treatments.notes: Cats with pre-existing bowel disease are at higher risk for complications and may require more symptomatic support.
